content: The document titled Core questions and indicators for monitoring WASH in health care facilities in the Sustainable Development Goals was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) in 2018. It is protected under a Creative Commons license, which allows for non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation of the content, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of WHO or UNICEF names and logos is not permitted, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, a disclaimer must be included stating that neither WHO nor UNICEF is responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The publication emphasizes the critical importance of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in health care facilities (HCFs) for delivering safe and quality health care. It highlights the significant gaps in WASH services, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, where many facilities lack even basic water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure. This deficiency compromises the ability to provide routine health services and to prevent and control infections. Without adequate WASH services in HCFs, global goals such as universal access to WASH, universal health coverage, and reductions in preventable newborn deaths and maternal mortality cannot be achieved. The document outlines the need for leadership from the health sector, technical expertise from the WASH sector, and political commitment from governments and non-governmental organizations to improve WASH services in HCFs. It also stresses the importance of harmonized monitoring and data collection to track progress and ensure accountability. The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) has developed a set of core indicators and questions to support the monitoring of WASH in HCFs in alignment with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. These indicators define basic levels of water, sanitation, hygiene, health care waste management, and environmental cleaning services. The core questions and indicators are designed to be applicable across different data collection mechanisms, relevant in all countries and settings, and focused on the minimum criteria for basic WASH services in HCFs. They aim to facilitate harmonized data collection, enabling better comparison of survey results over time and across countries. This harmonization will also support global analysis of WASH in HCFs within the context of the 2030 Agenda. The document acknowledges the contributions of the WASH in HCF Expert Group and the Global Task Team on monitoring WASH in HCFs in the SDG era. These groups played a significant role in developing the harmonized core questions and indicators. The publication also recognizes the efforts of various individuals and organizations who participated in expert group meetings and webinars to refine the indicators and questions. The publication notes that current data on WASH in HCFs is limited, with significant gaps in global coverage estimates. A 2015 WHO and UNICEF report found that nearly 40% of HCFs lacked a water supply within 500 meters, 19% lacked access to improved sanitation, and 35% had no handwashing facilities. Many assessments were not nationally representative, and definitions of WASH in HCFs often fell short of WHO minimum standards. This lack of standardized data limits the ability to establish accurate national trends and cross-country comparisons, as well as regional and global aggregation. To address these challenges, the document proposes a set of core and expanded questions for use in surveys, censuses, and health management information systems (HMIS). These questions are intended to capture data on basic WASH services and allow for more detailed assessments of additional criteria beyond the basic service level. The core questions are designed to be suitable for use in different formats, with some variations in formulation depending on whether they are completed by administrators or trained enumerators. The publication concludes by emphasizing the importance of harmonized questions in health care facility surveys to generate globally comparable data for monitoring WASH in HCFs. It highlights the need for alignment of existing data sources with the core indicators to establish SDG baseline estimates and improve the accuracy of national, regional, and global analyses.
